implementation_notes: Swift 5.5 made actors a language feature: an actor is a reference type whose mutable state is protected by actor isolation, and a cross-actor call becomes an asynchronous message placed in the actor's mailbox and processed one at a time - SE-0306 states the mailbox and the one-at-a-time execution explicitly and notes the implementation is a serial executor rather than a strict FIFO queue. What replaces the classic structure: the actor keyword, await, and the Sendable rules, which reject sharing non-Sendable references across isolation boundaries so the no-shared-mutable-state rule is compiler-checked. Before Swift 5.5 the effect was emulated with a serial DispatchQueue and a lock-free state class; keep that only where the deployment target cannot move.
pitfalls: Actors are reentrant: a suspension point (await) inside an actor method lets the next message run, so invariants checked before the await may be stale after it - SE-0306 discusses reentrancy and the deadlocks of non-reentrant designs at length.
Cross-actor calls must involve Sendable types; returning a mutable class reference is a compile error, and working around it smuggles shared state out of the actor.
Mailbox order is not FIFO across callers because the serial executor uses priority escalation and reordering, so arrival order must not be part of the protocol.
Frequent small cross-actor calls pay a hop each; batch work into fewer messages instead of one call per field.
